setInfo: CoroCoro Comic #223 glossy promo (unnumbered), Japan

estimatedValue: Enormous but volatile — sealed CoroCoro #223 issues have been valued near $150,000, while peeled singles vary wildly with condition

setInfo: No trading card release — and there never will be

noCardReason: Bill Watterson refused to licence Calvin and Hobbes for merchandise of any kind, won legal control of licensing from his syndicate in 1991, and has never granted a card deal. This is the rare case where the absence is a decision rather than an oversight.

A DC hero runs down the front; two other characters hide on the flaps, so one card refolds into nine mismatched figures. setInfo: 1993 Topps Batman: The Animated Series #36, "Harley Quinn"
description: Harley was written for a single episode of Batman: The Animated Series, "Joker's Favor", broadcast on 11 September 1992. She would not appear in a comic until 1993's Mad Love, so the card arrived at roughly the same moment as the character's move into print.
funFacts: She is one of very few major DC characters whose first card predates her first comic appearance, because she was invented for television rather than for the page

Her comic debut followed within the same year — The Batman Adventures #12, September 1993 — and Mad Love came in February 1994

setInfo: 1988 Comic Images "World of Spider-Man" sticker #50
description: Venom was only months old when this came out — he had taken proper form in Amazing Spider-Man #300 in May 1988 — and Comic Images put him at the very end of its fifty-sticker Spider-Man set the same year. Sticker #50 is the symbiote head alone against a yellow crescent, jaw open, tongue out. The stickers measure 2 x 3 inches, came four to a pack, and were split across six different frame designs; this one uses the black "Brickwork" border.
funFacts: The stickers carry a number on the front but no title at all — the only text printed on #50 is "TM & © 1988 MARVEL ENT. GP., INC.", so the name Venom comes from graders and databases rather than from the set itself
Collation on the set was dreadful: the collector who documented it bought a complete sealed box, got a dozen copies of sticker #1 and not a single #50
It is routinely mis-credited. Sellers who know the set advertise it as the "true RC, not 1989" — the 1989 Comic Images Todd McFarlane #3 and the 1990 Impel Marvel Universe I #73 are both later
estimatedValue: Raw copies sell at $225 – $400 on recent sold listings.

setInfo: 1938 Castell Brothers "Shuffled Symphonies", "Goofy" (red- and blue-backed twin packs)
description: Goofy had been on screen since 1932, first as Dippy Dawg, and spent the whole of the thirties without a card — he is absent from the 1935 Gum, Inc. Mickey Mouse set, whose supporting cast runs to Minnie, Pluto, Horace Horsecollar and Clarabelle Cow and stops there. He finally turns up in Britain, in a Castell Brothers card game of 45 cards covering twenty-two Disney characters, standing in his red shirt and patched blue trousers with his name printed along the bottom edge.
funFacts: The 1935 Gum, Inc. R89 set and its R90 continuation between them run to 120 cards without a single Goofy, which is how a character six years into his career ended up with a British card game for a rookie
The card names him on the front, which matters here: the project's recurring trap is sets where the checklist title and the figure pictured are not the same thing
Sellers who know the set advertise it as his rookie outright — "GOOFY ROOKIE 1ST DISNEY CARD 1938 CASTELL SHUFFLED SYMPHONIES"

The year is contested within one source: Collecting Pepys dates the game 1938 on its own page, citing a Daily Herald advertisement of 23 November 1938, but lists it as 1939 on its Disney overview page. The dated newspaper advert is the stronger evidence
estimatedValue: $25 – $150 raw depending on condition and back colour, with the better copies at the top of that band

setInfo: Gum, Inc. Superman (R145) #12 'Superman's Arch Enemy'
description: Lex Luthor's first card is #12 of the same 1940 Gum, Inc. set that carries Superman's own first card, #1 — the two debuted on cardboard together, not years apart. The front is titled 'Superman's Arch Enemy' rather than naming him, though the back does name him. The figure at the control panel is drawn with a full head of red hair, the way Luthor was shown before the bald design settled in, and collectors routinely list the card as a rookie without saying whose.

Drawn with a full head of red hair, years before the bald Luthor became standard
Shares its set and its year with Superman's own rookie, card #1 of the same 72-card release
